title: Region-aware load sculpting and TTL strategy for multi-region steering
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a concrete pattern for combining region-aware traffic shaping ("load sculpting") with DNS/Anycast TTL policies and control-plane decisioning to meet multi-region SLOs while preserving operational stability and predictable cost. The goal is an implementable design that balances fast failover, per-region capacity limits, and reasonable DNS churn for end users and partner integrations.

Context and constraints:
- We operate in ~6 regions with capacity variance per region (gpu pools differ).
- Clients expect sub-200ms p95 for small-chat requests; larger prompt latencies are elastic but still routed for locality when possible.
- We must avoid overloading smaller regions during global traffic spikes while keeping hot-user affinity intact for cache/KV reuse.
- Some customers require session affinity (private deployments), others tolerate best-effort routing.
- We have both GeoDNS and Anycast-capable edges; control-plane must orchestrate both where available.

Design principles (short):
- Prefer local-region routing when capacity headroom exists and latency penalty is < SLO delta.
- Sculpt excess traffic proactively at the control-plane rather than relying solely on DNS failover.
- Keep DNS TTLs long enough to reduce global churn but short enough to support rollouts and recovery when we intentionally re-route.
- Use probes + telemetry to drive region ejection and re-inclusion with hysteresis.

Key primitives we will use:
- GeoDNS: per-zone records with weighted answers and optional EDNS-client-subnet hints where supported.
- Anycast: global IPs with regional origin preference via BGP communities and local preference adjustments when necessary.
- Control-plane policy service: admits per-customer and global steering policies, exports routing hints to DNS/Anycast controllers and edge proxies.
- Region ejection controller: ingest region metrics (utilization, queue length, p95 latency, error rate, cost delta) and emit state (healthy, degraded, ejected, probed).
- Load-sculptor: token-bucket per-region + per-customer soft-limits; returns routing decision or suggested fallback.

High-level flow:
1) Ingest telemetry (1s granularity) into steering control plane (aggregated per region, per model, per customer tier).
2) Decision engine computes region health and computes target weights for GeoDNS answers and Anycast origin pulls.
3) Load-sculptor enforces hard caps (protect control-plane & underlying GPU pools) and returns either accept, accept-with-delay (queue), or redirect-to-fallback.
4) DNS/Anycast controllers reconcile weights and origin hints every reconciliation window (configurable).
5) Prober subsystem validates ejected regions before promoting them back (see probe policy).

TTL strategy (practical defaults):
- Global default TTL = 300s (5m) for public hosted API records. Rationale: balance between agility and DNS load.
- During controlled canary/rollout: TTL = 60s for affected records only.
- On emergency failover (region ejection): proactively lower TTL to 30s for affected prefixes for a short window (max 10m) while control-plane stabilizes.
- For enterprise customers using dedicated endpoints: TTL can be higher (1h) if customer requests, and we rely on connection-level routing (sticky proxy).

Why not always use short TTL?
- Very short TTLs increase global DNS query QPS and make external resolvers more likely to ignore TTLs; many CDNs and resolvers enforce minimums. 300s is a pragmatic median.

Load-sculpting heuristics (examples):
- Soft limit: region capacity * 0.85 -> start returning 429-backpressure responses to best-effort clients and trigger traffic redistribution for routable requests.
- Hard limit: region capacity * 0.95 -> immediate ejection flag set; control-plane will reduce GeoDNS/Anycast weight to ~0 over multiple reconciliation ticks and instruct edge proxies to refuse new connections for non-sticky flows.
- Graceful drain: after marking ejected, allow inflight requests up to 60s completion window (configurable by model).
- Per-customer override: enterprise contracts can pin to region with higher hard limits (and billing adjustments).

Probe + re-inclusion policy:
- After ejection, mark region as probed. Prober performs low-rate synthetic traffic from multiple vantage points (internal probe agents) to detect recovery across both latency and correctness (model outputs healthy).
- Re-inclusion requires: 3 consecutive probe passes within probe-window (default 3m) and stabilization of primary metrics (p95 within 10% of baseline and error-rate < threshold).
- Use staggered ramp-up (10% -> 30% -> 70% -> baseline) over multiple reconciliation ticks to avoid thundering herd.

Affinity and cache/KV considerations (LLM-specific):
- KV cache locality is important for long chats. For sticks: prefer per-client cookie or per-api-key affinity keyed to consistent-hash region assignment.
- When redirecting for failover, include a “cache-warm” hint: edge proxies add a sequence of prefetch requests (low-priority) to warm remote caches where appropriate. Limit to enterprise customers.

Anycast vs GeoDNS coordination:
- Primary mode: prefer Anycast for read-heavy low-latency paths where BGP engineering provides stable locality. Use GeoDNS weight adjustments as the control-plane source-of-truth for origin preferences in cases where Anycast can be de-preferenced (via communities) per region.
- If Anycast global routes are blackholed or asymmetric, GeoDNS fallback provides per-client resolver-level steering. Control-plane must detect BGP-origin anomalies and switch to GeoDNS-dominant mode for affected prefixes.

Metrics to drive decisions (ingested at 1s-10s resolution):
- p50/p90/p95 latency per region/model/customer
- queued_requests and queue_latency per region
- GPU_utilization, GPU_mem_pressure per pool
- request_error_rate (5xx, 4xx) and model-inference-failures
- DNS QPS and Anycast origin churn rate (per prefix)
- egress_cost_estimate (per-region) for cost-aware steering

Operational playbooks (short):
- Routine spike: control-plane will first begin load-sculpting (soft limit) then adjust GeoDNS weights. Ops alert if >2 regions enter hard-limit at once.
- Region outage: mark ejected, set TTL 30s for affected records, start prober and routing-weight ramp to fallback regions. Notify on-call and customers with affected SLAs.
- Rollback of steering change: use canary TTLs and slow ramp; rollback will restore previous weights and set TTL back to default.

Migration plan and experiments:
- Week 0–2: Simulate spikes using internal traffic generator and validate load-sculptor thresholds.
- Week 3–4: Enable control-plane-driven GeoDNS weight adjustments for non-critical prefixes with short TTL canary.
- Week 5–6: Enable Anycast origin hints for 2 prefixes; measure egress cost and latency changes.
- KPI: reduce cross-region failover latency by >30% for canary workloads and avoid increase in global DNS QPS beyond 2x baseline.

Open questions / risks:
- EDNS-client-subnet adoption and accuracy across resolvers: how reliably can we rely on it for fine-grained steering?
- Resolver TTL behavior: large public resolvers may ignore TTLs below certain thresholds, complicating fast rollbacks.
- Interaction with third-party CDNs that front our endpoints (need mapping and sync).
- Billing complexity when per-customer regional pinning leads to capacity fragmentation.

Next actions (owners):
- (Aisha) Draft steering API schema for per-prefix weights and region-policy flags (PLAT-2893).
- (Marco) Prototype load-sculptor sidecar for region pools and simulate under synthetic traffic (PR #412).
- (Sofia) Run DNS/Anycast reconciliation chaos tests in staging (tickets + runbook).
- (Priya) Measure real resolver TTL behaviors across 10 public resolvers and publish findings.
